newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Gunfire breaks out at Albania royalist rally.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire breaks out at Albania royalist rally.

text.p: Shooting erupted in central Tirana on Thursday during a march organised by monarchist supporters of exiled king Leka and at least one person appeared to have been injured.
Around 500 supporters of the king, who was wants to restored to the throne were involved in the march from the main Skanderbeg Square down a main boulevard past government buildings.
Firing broke out as the marchers converged on the election headquarters, denouncing results from a referendum showing voters had rejected ditching the republic to re-establish a monarchy.

Leka, who has spent most of his life in Europe and South Africa, strode through the gathering in battle fatigues and a grey beret towards the headquarters of the central electoral commission, which is still compiling final results of Sunday's general election.

Supporters shouted slogans against Socialist leader Fatos Nano, whose party has defeated President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party. Berisha has already conceded defeat despite a second round of voting on Sunday.
Witnesses said the shooting, which reverberated for around 10 minutes, appeared to be aimed in the air.
Volleys of gunfire from automatic rifles and small arms could be heard next to an international hotel where foreign observers and reporters are staying.
Both marchers, passers-by and journalists scattered behind buildings and vehicles as soon as the gunfire erupted.
A handful of police appeared powerless to take any action.

A spokesman in the central electoral commission building, which had some of its windows shot out, said no-one had been hurt inside. Relative calm returned but security forces in the street shouted at people to hurry inside buildings.

Leka has insisted a referendum on restoring the monarchy was supported by the majority of voters on Sunday, But the central electoral commission said on Wednesday around 35.7 percent voted in favour of the king and some 64.2 percent against.
